about.title: San Fernando Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast, but the aftermath rarely feels that way. Whether the incident took place inside a business near Truman Street, in a parking lot off Glenoaks Boulevard, or on a poorly maintained walkway near N Maclay Avenue, the property owner's responsibility depends on what they knew, or should have known, about the hazard. San Fernando's mix of small commercial strips, older apartment buildings, and busy retail corridors means uneven pavement, wet floors, and poor lighting are common triggers for these claims. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your case directly; instead, we connect you with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate what happened, help you gather evidence, and explain your options under California law. Because evidence like surveillance footage often disappears within days or weeks, reaching out promptly matters far more than most people realize.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a San Fernando Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California law generally requires showing the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and failed to fix or warn about it. An attorney can help identify maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that support this.

items.title: Acting Before Evidence Disappears
items.desc: Security footage from stores or apartment complexes near corridors like San Fernando Road is often overwritten within days. Getting documentation and witness statements early can make a real difference later.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning any partial responsibility you might share doesn't automatically bar a claim, though it can reduce recovery. An attorney can help explain how this applies to your specific situation.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in San Fernando?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit, though claims against a public entity, like a city-owned sidewalk, often require faster action, sometimes within six months. It's best to confirm timing with an attorney soon after the incident. Waiting too long can limit your options.

items.question: What if the fall happened at a business along Truman Street or Glenoaks Boulevard?
items.answer: Businesses along these corridors have a duty to maintain reasonably safe conditions for customers. If a hazard like a spill or broken tile existed long enough that staff should have noticed it, that can support a claim. An attorney can help request incident reports and any available video from the business.

items.question: Do I need proof the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, California premises liability generally requires showing the owner had actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition. This might come from prior complaints, repair records, or how long the hazard existed before your fall. Documenting the scene with photos right away can help preserve this evidence.
